transcript.speaker: moderator
transcript.text: Hello, and welcome. I'm joined by our Technical Lead and Mentor, and we're excited to hear about your work. Could you describe a technical project you've built, focusing on the problem, the architecture, and your specific contribution?

transcript.speaker: candidate
transcript.text: At the University of Waterloo, supervised by Professor Sebastian Fischmeister, I researched retrieval poisoning attacks against RAG-based code generation. The question was whether poisoned documents in a retrieval store can push a model into generating bad code. I built an OpenSSL document store and evaluated 58 adversarial documents across 14,218 C functions. I also built a top-k vector retrieval pipeline with OpenAI's text-embedding-3-large and fine-tuned MPNet embeddings. Then I ran paired clean-versus-poisoned code generation experiments with GPT-4.1 and GPT-5, and checked the generated functions with compilation, the OpenSSL unit tests, memory analysis and fuzz testing. My main contribution was choosing canary functions: a linear regression on code distance, function length, brace depth and fan-in finds the functions most sensitive to a poisoned store.

transcript.speaker: technical_lead
transcript.text: Thanks for the overview. Let's get started.

transcript.speaker: technical_lead
transcript.text: How did you choose the four features for the canary regression?

transcript.speaker: candidate
transcript.text: I started from what makes a function depend on retrieved context. Longer functions and deeper nesting give the model more places to copy a bad pattern, and fan-in tells you how many callers would be hit. Code distance is how close the function is to the poisoned documents in embedding space. I tried about ten features and kept the four with significant coefficients.

transcript.speaker: technical_lead
transcript.text: How many of the adversarial documents were actually retrieved for at least one function?

transcript.speaker: candidate
transcript.text: Most of them. Out of the 120 adversarial documents, I think around 90 were retrieved at least once in the top five.

transcript.speaker: mentor
transcript.text: That's completely fine. Let's move on.

transcript.speaker: mentor
transcript.text: How did you check that watching the canaries caught a poisoned store sooner than checking every function?

transcript.speaker: moderator
transcript.text: That's all from our panel today. Thank you so much for walking us through your project, and best of luck!
